interpretation: Each thing is most such, compared with the others, when the synonymous quality belongs to the others in virtue of it (καθʼ ὃ καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις ὑπάρχει τὸ συνώνυμον): fire, the cause of heat to the others, is hottest; so what causes the posterior things to be true is most true. 'Most such' (μάλιστα) is weakened faithfully to the pairwise comparative. Reading step, stated as a strengthening: the bound statement says it of every cause of a quality in another (CausesIn), not only of the cause that has the quality synonymously, so it also covers equivocal or analogical causes, which the sentence does not; the attribution to Aristotle covers only the synonymous-cause instance, and the extension is an unattributed open strengthening (audit B; a weaker sibling statement with a synonymous-cause condition is a recorded follow-up). The text does not itself say that a cause of another's being is more a being: 993b26-31 concludes that the principles of the eternal beings are most true and that as each thing stands to being, so to truth (claim ARIST-MET-993B-AS-TO-BEING-SO-TO-TRUTH-A). The reading gives no step from causing one quality to being more in another, so it bears on simple priority only through the separate open premise STMT-SIMPLY-PRIOR-IS-CAUSE-OF-BEING. Aquinas cites this chapter in the quarta via for the converse (the maximum causes all in its genus), recorded in AQUINAS-ST-I-Q2-A3-MAXIMUM-CAUSES-GENUS-A.
